ocar.opportunity: Super-resolution light microscopy can visualize molecules and individual cells at nanoscale, but maps of dense brain architecture also need tissue context from regional to synaptic scales.
ocar.challenge: Labeled optical readouts typically miss unlabeled neighbors, so they fail to provide the dense context that electron microscopy supplies, especially in chemically fixed rodent and human tissue.
ocar.action: Michalska, Lyudchik, Velicky, and colleagues, in a 2022 bioRxiv preprint, introduce Comprehensive Analysis of Tissues across Scales (CATS): fixation-compatible extracellular labeling read out with stimulated-emission depletion and expansion microscopy.
ocar.resolution: CATS densely maps architecture from millimeter regional to nanoscopic synaptic scales in chemically fixed rodent and human brain, reconstructing single synapses via putative synaptic clefts. Applied to hippocampal mossy-fiber circuitry, it reconstructs and quantifies synaptic input and output of identified neurons in a molecularly informed ultrastructure.
ocar.future_work: The extract documents human surgical specimens, cerebral organoids, and patch-clamp as complementary readouts; a full comparison of CATS clefts with EM-defined synapses across circuits is not a completed census in this preprint.

summaries.beginner: Super-resolution light microscopy usually sees labeled cells, not the whole dense neighborhood. This preprint introduces CATS, which stains the spaces around cells so researchers can map brain tissue from large regions down to individual synapses, including in human samples.
summaries.intermediate: Michalska and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2022) present CATS, combining extracellular labeling compatible with chemical fixation with STED and expansion microscopy. They argue this densely delineates cellular structures from millimeter to synaptic scales in rodent and human preparations, and they reconstruct putative synaptic clefts in 3D. The demonstration is hippocampal mossy-fiber circuitry, including input and output structure of identified neurons. Human neurosurgical tissue and organoids appear as additional preparations rather than a whole-brain human connectome.
summaries.advanced: This is a bioRxiv preprint (CC-BY-NC-ND), not a peer-reviewed final version. 'Putative synaptic clefts' are optical, not an EM gold standard. The selected extract’s closing pages are acknowledgements and author contributions; synapse counts are not stated as single summary statistics in the provided text. PSD95-HaloTag mice are noted as a reagent.

plain_language_summary: Super-resolution light microscopy usually sees labeled cells, not the whole dense neighborhood. This preprint introduces CATS, which stains the spaces around cells so researchers can map brain tissue from large regions down to individual synapses, including in human samples.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila larvae are a standard genetic model, but driver-line expression is usually documented only inside one organ of interest rather than across the whole body.
ocar.challenge: Larvae are small yet cuticularized, so clearing is error-prone; toxic solvents and enzymatic digestion of the exoskeleton hinder routine whole-body fluorescence imaging.
ocar.action: Kobler, Weiglein, Hartung, Chen, Gerber, and Thomas, in Journal of Neurogenetics (2021), report a larva-specific, low-toxicity clearing protocol using brief bleach and ethyl cinnamate (ECi) instead of more toxic agents such as DBE or THF.
ocar.resolution: The protocol supports light-sheet and confocal imaging at cellular resolution with a success rate they consider high enough for small-scale screens. Membrane-tethered mCherry-CAAX and soluble monomeric infrared fluorescent protein (mIFP) performed well, enabling triple-color near-infrared, red, and yellow volumes. They document nsyb-Gal4, IR76b-Gal4, APL/mushroom-body Kenyon cells, and OK371-Gal4 in whole larval bodies.
ocar.future_work: DsRed after clearing was unsatisfactory. The authors suggest trying additional red-shifted reporters and using the method to extend existing driver-line documentation systematically to the whole body.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae are easy to genetically label, but published pictures usually show only one organ. This paper gives a fast, relatively non-toxic way to make the whole larva clear so many fluorescent labels can be seen at once.
summaries.intermediate: Kobler et al. (Journal of Neurogenetics, 2021; catalog row listed as bioRxiv) optimize whole-body multi-fluorescence imaging of third-instar Drosophila larvae. Brief bleach replaces enzymatic cuticle digestion, and ECi is used as a budget, non-toxic organic clearer suited to lipid-rich fat body. They highlight mIFP and mCherry-CAAX, show triple-color volumes, and place pan-neuronal and subset driver patterns (including motor neurons labeled by OK371-Gal4) in the intact body. The catalog journal field does not match the published PDF venue.
summaries.advanced: The PDF is the published Journal of Neurogenetics article, not a bioRxiv file. Claims about screening suitability and cellular resolution are the authors’ qualitative assessments. Scale bars in the extract (200 µm / 50 µm) are figure annotations, not protocol timings. No synapse-level connectome is produced.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae are easy to genetically label, but published pictures usually show only one organ. This paper gives a fast, relatively non-toxic way to make the whole larva clear so many fluorescent labels can be seen at once.

ocar.opportunity: If gene-regulatory networks are modular, transcriptome graphs might recover mesoscale brain circuits without starting from tracer or imaging connectomes.
ocar.challenge: There is no standard bottom-up path from gene communities across regions to region-level modules that can be read as a mesoconnectome.
ocar.action: Paredes, López, Covantes-Osuna, Ocegueda-Hernández, Romo-Vázquez, and Morales, in Entropy (2021), estimate gene communities from the Allen Brain Atlas transcriptome and assemble brain-wide region modules.
ocar.resolution: They select a community method meant to maximize functional mesostructures and report communities associated with neuroplasticity, axonogenesis, and dendritogenesis. Resulting modules are said to match previously described circuits, including the default mode network and default visual network, supporting the claim that low- and higher-order dynamics originate from modular GRN composition.
ocar.future_work: The extract notes low statistical power for inter-subject modules. Data Availability is listed as not applicable; the work is a modeling study on public atlas data.

summaries.beginner: This paper tries to guess how human brain regions group into circuits by looking at which genes turn on together, not by tracing axons. The authors say some of those gene-based groups look like networks already known from imaging, such as the default mode network.
summaries.intermediate: Paredes et al. (Entropy, 2021) propose a gene-regulatory-network-to-mesoconnectome workflow on Allen Brain Atlas transcriptome data. Graph communities of genes are built across regions, then used to form region modules interpreted as a connectome. Matches to default mode and default visual networks are presented as support that brain dynamics arise from modular GRN structure. This is computational inference from expression, not a new tract-tracing or EM map.
summaries.advanced: Causal language linking GRN modules to dynamics is interpretive. ‘Default visual network’ is the authors’ phrasing. No new empirical connectivity measurements are reported. A limitations passage flags low power for inter-subject modules.

plain_language_summary: This paper tries to guess how human brain regions group into circuits by looking at which genes turn on together, not by tracing axons. The authors say some of those gene-based groups look like networks already known from imaging, such as the default mode network.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can show synapses, glia, vessels, and organelles in one volume, so degeneration can be read as both wiring change and subcellular pathology.
ocar.challenge: Classic EM samples tiny areas; imaging and reconstructing entire volumes is impractical when many diseased retinas must be compared.
ocar.action: Zucker and Dowling, in a Neural Regeneration Research perspective (2022 print of a 2021 DOI), describe targeted high-throughput serial-section SEM of macular telangiectasia (MacTel) retina using automated tape-collecting ultramicrotomy.
ocar.resolution: They describe collecting on the order of 10,000–15,000 sections about 30 nm thick from a block covering up to about 3.5 mm × 6 mm and about one-third of a millimeter thick, then using overview images of every 100th section to guide high-resolution single-beam or 61-beam SEM. In MacTel they report disordered photoreceptor outer-segment discs, swollen empty mitochondria in ellipsoids, and a circumscribed transition zone between profound degeneration and subtler mitochondrial change with near-normal circuitry.
ocar.future_work: They argue that restorative efforts should be judged by whether damaged circuitry can be rolled back in a functionally meaningful way, and that full-volume ‘traditional’ connectomics of every sample is not practical.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopy can show every connection and organelle in a piece of retina, which matters in diseases that destroy photoreceptors. This short perspective explains how large serial-section volumes are used to study macular telangiectasia, including a border zone where damage is still spreading.
summaries.intermediate: Zucker and Dowling (Neural Regeneration Research, 2022) review serial-section EM connectomics and apply it to MacTel retina. ATUM-style collection of tens of thousands of 30 nm sections from a multi-millimeter block lets them navigate X/Y/Z and zoom to high resolution. They highlight photoreceptor ellipsoid mitochondria and a transition zone between severe and subtle pathology. The piece is a perspective citing their 2020 targeted-connectomics work, not a full methods paper.
summaries.advanced: Two-column layout in the extract mixes adjacent columns; only numbers and MacTel claims that appear in coherent sentences were used (section counts, 30 nm, ~3.5 mm × 6 mm, ~1/3 mm thickness). Catalog abstract is more generic about 4 nm resolution (citing Kasthuri et al. 2015). Müller glia/serine remarks in the extract are too jumbled to treat as quantified results.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopy can show every connection and organelle in a piece of retina, which matters in diseases that destroy photoreceptors. This short perspective explains how large serial-section volumes are used to study macular telangiectasia, including a border zone where damage is still spreading.

ocar.opportunity: Dense reconstructions from volume EM can reveal higher-order wiring that sparse sampling misses, which may be essential for computation.
ocar.challenge: Wiring diagrams alone do not explain function without activity and behavior, and combining those measurements has been hard in most species.
ocar.action: Friedrich and Wanner, in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2021), review dynamical connectomics in zebrafish: dense circuit reconstruction together with population activity and behavior.
ocar.resolution: They highlight three cases: recurrently connected brainstem modules that can account for slow, low-dimensional integrator dynamics; spinal connectivity that specifies functional differences among premotor interneurons; and tuning-dependent olfactory-bulb connectivity that implements whitening by suppressing responses to overrepresented stimulus features. Small brain size is argued to enable cross-area maps and reconstructions of equivalent circuits in multiple individuals, including adult brain areas.
ocar.future_work: Named next steps include relating neurite and synapse ultrastructure to weights and gene expression, and mapping interindividual and experience-dependent wiring variation. They emphasize that vEM volumes contain more than graphs.

summaries.beginner: Complete wiring diagrams from electron microscopy are most useful when they can be matched to how neurons fire and how the animal behaves. This review argues that larval and adult zebrafish are well suited to that combination, and it walks through examples in brainstem, spinal cord, and olfactory bulb.
summaries.intermediate: Friedrich and Wanner (Annual Review of Neuroscience, 2021) survey dense EM reconstruction plus activity as ‘dynamical connectomics,’ focused on zebrafish. Examples are a brainstem integrator, spinal premotor interneurons, and olfactory-bulb whitening. They argue sparse connectivity samples miss higher-order structure needed for computation, while wiring without dynamics is still insufficient. Outlook includes multi-individual maps and ultrastructure–transcriptome links.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not a new reconstruction. Computational interpretations (integrator dynamics, whitening) summarize cited primary papers. Expected publication date language in the catalog abstract is boilerplate. The PDF extract includes publisher download headers.

plain_language_summary: Complete wiring diagrams from electron microscopy are most useful when they can be matched to how neurons fire and how the animal behaves. This review argues that larval and adult zebrafish are well suited to that combination, and it walks through examples in brainstem, spinal cord, and olfactory bulb.

ocar.opportunity: Wide-field microscopy images large brain volumes faster than confocal, which could support reconstruction of long neurites if segmentation, visualization, and serial-section alignment work together.
ocar.challenge: Physically sectioned samples sit at arbitrary poses; micrometer-scale neurites are hard to annotate, automatically segment, and stitch across cuts.
ocar.action: Ghahremani, Boorboor, Mirhosseini, Gudisagar, Ananth, Talmage, Role, and Kaufman, in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2022 publication of a 2021 DOI), introduce NeuroConstruct, an end-to-end application for wide-field volumes.
ocar.resolution: A Segmentation Toolbox supports expert annotation and trains a CNN for neurites, with somas segmented by thresholding. Hybrid rendering combines iso-surfaces of high-confidence neurites with a 2D transfer function of classification score versus intensity. A Registration Toolbox performs coarse-to-fine alignment of serial sections, including rigid transforms from interfacing z-slices using Mattes mutual information. The authors claim it outperforms prior methods and apply it to cholinergic neurons relevant to Alzheimer’s disease. Imaging a 40× slice is stated as 1.5 hours on wide-field versus 15 hours confocal.
ocar.future_work: The extract flags retraining the model on annotations refined in hybrid visualization mode as future work against remaining segmentation limits.

summaries.beginner: Wide-field microscopes can photograph large pieces of brain quickly, but tracing thin nerve fibers across cut slices is still hard. NeuroConstruct is a software suite meant to help people label those fibers, have a network finish the tracing, and glue the slices back into one 3D picture.
summaries.intermediate: Ghahremani et al. (IEEE TVCG, 2022; DOI 2021) present NeuroConstruct for segmentation, registration, and visualization of wide-field optical volumes. CNNs trained on toolbox annotations segment neurites; somas use thresholding; visualization is hybrid iso-surface plus transfer function; registration uses tissue-structure rigid alignment to a user-chosen reference section. The motivating biology is cholinergic axons in Alzheimer’s-related studies. Quantitative ‘outperforms state-of-the-art in all design aspects’ is the authors’ summary claim.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript, not the publisher PDF. ‘Outperforms SOTA in all design aspects’ is not accompanied by a single numeric leaderboard in the selected extract. Confocal versus wide-field times (15 h vs 1.5 h) are stated for a 40× slice in the extract. Application is optical morphology, not EM synapses.

plain_language_summary: Wide-field microscopes can photograph large pieces of brain quickly, but tracing thin nerve fibers across cut slices is still hard. NeuroConstruct is a software suite meant to help people label those fibers, have a network finish the tracing, and glue the slices back into one 3D picture.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans combines a complete neuronal connectome with tractable genetics, so it is a place to ask how neuropeptides retune wired circuits into flexible behavior.
ocar.challenge: How small peptides shape feeding, mating, sleep, addiction, learning, and locomotion, and how those pathways relate to conserved disease biology, is scattered across many studies.
ocar.action: Bhat, Shahi, Surendran, and Babu, in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience (2021), review neuropeptidergic modulation of those behaviors in C. elegans and conserved peptide functions across phyla.
ocar.resolution: The review synthesizes mechanisms of neuropeptide signaling and their regulation across the named behaviors, treating the connectome as anatomical context for extrasynaptic and synaptic peptide action. Insight into therapeutics for neuropeptide-related disorders is offered as an outlook, not as new clinical data.
ocar.future_work: Translating worm peptide pathways into medicines remains prospective. The piece is a literature synthesis, not a new map or screen.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram is famous, but much of behavior is also shaped by small signaling peptides that are not ordinary fast synapses. This review collects how those peptides change feeding, mating, sleep, learning, and movement.
summaries.intermediate: Bhat et al. (Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience, 2021) review C. elegans neuropeptides as modulators of synaptic signaling and behavior, with emphasis on feeding, mating, sleep, addiction, learning, and locomotion. They discuss evolutionary conservation and pathophysiology and close by pointing toward therapeutics. The connectome is invoked as a reason the worm is a good model, not re-derived here.
summaries.advanced: Narrative review. Therapeutic language is speculative. Catalog tags include the White-era C. elegans dataset; this paper does not produce a new connectome. Conclusion restates that neuropeptides regulate behavior without new quantitative circuit statistics in the extract.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram is famous, but much of behavior is also shaped by small signaling peptides that are not ordinary fast synapses. This review collects how those peptides change feeding, mating, sleep, learning, and movement.

ocar.opportunity: A complete peripheral circuit plus activity recordings could show whether a learning principle predicts the synapse weights seen in a connectome.
ocar.challenge: Olfactory receptor-neuron activity is correlated, which is bad for discrimination, and how larval Drosophila inhibitory local neurons implement preprocessing was incomplete.
ocar.action: Chapochnikov, Pehlevan, and Chklovskii, in PNAS (2023 version of a 2021 DOI), combine Drosophila larva olfactory structure and activity in a similarity-matching framework, with an exactly solvable linear circuit and a nonnegative circuit model.
ocar.resolution: The nonnegative model largely predicts ORN→LN synaptic weights in the connectome as reflecting correlations in ORN activity, and accounts for relationships between ORN→LN and LN–LN synaptic counts and for LN types. They propose that LNs encode soft cluster memberships of ORN activity and partially whiten and normalize ORN representations via inhibitory feedback, a motif that could arise by Hebbian plasticity.
ocar.future_work: The discussion asks why the resemblance is strong despite an imperfect odor dataset and why it is not stronger. LN roles in temporal bandwidth were not modeled. Noise, plasticity, and genetics in circuit shaping are named as open.

summaries.beginner: Fly-larva smell neurons send overlapping messages that are hard to tell apart. This theory paper argues that local inhibitory neurons learn those overlaps from activity, match the wiring in the connectome, and clean up the smell code before it goes deeper into the brain.
summaries.intermediate: Chapochnikov, Pehlevan, and Chklovskii (PNAS, 2023; catalog listed as bioRxiv) model the larval ORN–LN feedback circuit with similarity-matching. A nonnegative model predicts connectome ORN→LN weights from ORN correlations and relates those weights to LN–LN counts. Functionally they argue for partial whitening and normalization of ORN representations. Catalog journal does not match the published PDF.
summaries.advanced: Normative model plus simulations, not a new EM volume. Fit quality is described qualitatively (‘largely predicts,’ ‘key structural characteristics’). The odor dataset is acknowledged as an imperfect match to the true larval environment. Edited by Terrence Sejnowski; accepted May 2023.

plain_language_summary: Fly-larva smell neurons send overlapping messages that are hard to tell apart. This theory paper argues that local inhibitory neurons learn those overlaps from activity, match the wiring in the connectome, and clean up the smell code before it goes deeper into the brain.

ocar.opportunity: Sex differences in behavior might be encoded by the same neurons wired differently rather than by different cell types.
ocar.challenge: How much of dimorphic nociception in C. elegans is sensory transduction versus downstream network topology was unknown.
ocar.action: Pechuk, Salzberg, Goldman, and colleagues, in a 2021 bioRxiv preprint, map dimorphic nociceptive behavior, fit a network model that reproduces sex-specific responses, and experimentally test predicted rewirings.
ocar.resolution: Sensory transduction is similar between sexes; topology shapes behavior. Predicted subtle synaptic rewirings flipped behavior. The hermaphrodite circuit was more robust to change than the male circuit. Rewired males were compromised in finding mating partners when aversive cues were present, suggesting that topologies enabling efficient avoidance have a reproductive cost. Calcium imaging of AVA showed inter-individual variability, including some males with hermaphrodite-like activity.
ocar.future_work: Whether hermaphrodite robustness is non-autonomous (body-derived signals) or an unknown cell-autonomous path remains open. Mechanisms of AVA individuality are unclear.

summaries.beginner: Male and hermaphrodite worms can use the same pain-sensing cells but wire them differently, which changes how they avoid danger. This preprint shows that small rewiring can switch one sex’s behavior toward the other, and that making males more avoidant can hurt mating.
summaries.intermediate: Pechuk et al. (bioRxiv, 2021) study a C. elegans nociceptive circuit built from shared neurons with dimorphic topology. A fitted network model predicted rewirings that experimentally flipped behavior. They report greater robustness of the hermaphrodite circuit, a mating cost for rewired males in the presence of aversive cues, and variable AVA responses. The work treats topology, not transduction, as the main dimorphic cause.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint (CC-BY-NC-ND). ‘Subtle synaptic rewirings’ are not given as a single synapse-count table in the selected extract. Non-reciprocal sex-reversal results are contrasted with prior cell-autonomous sex-identity studies. Later journal version is not this file.

plain_language_summary: Male and hermaphrodite worms can use the same pain-sensing cells but wire them differently, which changes how they avoid danger. This preprint shows that small rewiring can switch one sex’s behavior toward the other, and that making males more avoidant can hurt mating.

ocar.opportunity: Balanced colorings and graph fibrations mark clusters that can synchronize, which may organize biological networks including neural connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Experimental networks are incomplete—missing links, errors, specimen variation—so true symmetries are under-detected.
ocar.action: Leifer, Phillips, Sorrentino, and Makse introduce the pseudobalanced coloring integer program (PBCIP), which colors a graph allowing for missing data and repairs it with a minimal number of added or removed edges to maximize symmetry, and apply it to the C. elegans connectome (Journal of Statistical Mechanics / arXiv 2021–2022).
ocar.resolution: The C. elegans repair is reported to compare well with a manually curated ground-truth graph and with other missing-link prediction methods. Bender’s decomposition is provided so the formulation can be applied to larger networks.
ocar.future_work: Interpreting repaired edges as biological versus artifactual, and scaling beyond the worm, are the intended uses. The selected PDF extract is largely the abstract plus table of contents, so detailed repair counts are not in the provided text.

summaries.beginner: Real wiring diagrams are missing some connections, which can hide repeating patterns in the network. This methods paper looks for almost-symmetries in the worm connectome and adds or deletes the fewest links needed to make those patterns complete.
summaries.intermediate: Leifer et al. (J. Stat. Mech. / arXiv, 2021–2022) formulate PBCIP: integer programming for a pseudobalanced coloring and for minimal edge edits that restore symmetry. They apply it to C. elegans and compare to a curated ground-truth graph and other link-prediction methods. Bender’s decomposition is the scaling strategy. This is network reconstruction from symmetry assumptions, not new EM.
summaries.advanced: Selected extract does not include the computational-results section (listed as starting p. 23 in the TOC). Do not treat ‘compares well’ as a numeric accuracy. Catalog year is 2021; the arXiv stamp on the PDF is v2, 3 Mar 2022.

plain_language_summary: Real wiring diagrams are missing some connections, which can hide repeating patterns in the network. This methods paper looks for almost-symmetries in the worm connectome and adds or deletes the fewest links needed to make those patterns complete.

ocar.opportunity: Morphology, synapse locations, and network paths are usually visualized separately, which makes it hard to ask how a circuit is laid out in space.
ocar.challenge: Interactive exploration of simple-to-medium connectomes on detailed neuron morphologies, with usable metaphors for synapses and paths, is not standard.
ocar.action: Galindo, Toharia, Robles, and Pastor, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2021), present SynCoPa, combining detailed morphologies with visual metaphors for synapses and interconnection paths, using Blue Brain Project data.
ocar.resolution: The tool is designed for hypotheses about spatial synapse distributions and morphology–connectivity relationships and is described as extendable to functional data from simulators such as NEURON and Arbor.
ocar.future_work: Named limits include tracing and positioning errors, filtering that currently maps attributes to colors only, particles drawn at uniform size despite varying neurite caliber, and a desire for quantitative analysis widgets.

summaries.beginner: A wiring list does not show where synapses sit on a neuron’s branches. SynCoPa is visualization software that draws those synapses and the paths between cells on detailed 3D neuron shapes so a circuit can be inspected by eye.
summaries.intermediate: Galindo et al. (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2021) introduce SynCoPa for interactive connectome-level exploration of simple-to-medium circuits. Synapses and paths are shown on reconstructed morphologies. Data are from the Blue Brain Project. The paper is a methods/visualization contribution, not a new biological circuit discovery. Four demo videos are provided as supplements.
summaries.advanced: No new EM segmentation. ‘Simple to medium complexity’ is not quantified as a neuron count in the extract. Extendability to simulators is prospective. Acknowledgements credit Raquel Jarillo for early visualization work.

plain_language_summary: A wiring list does not show where synapses sit on a neuron’s branches. SynCoPa is visualization software that draws those synapses and the paths between cells on detailed 3D neuron shapes so a circuit can be inspected by eye.

ocar.opportunity: Diffusion MRI tractography is the only noninvasive human structural connectome method, so its geometric biases need measuring where tracers exist.
ocar.challenge: Length-dependent mistracking is confounded by the true contribution of spatial embedding to brain topology.
ocar.action: Trinkle, Foxley, Wildenberg, Kasthuri, and La Rivière, in NeuroImage (2021), compare ex vivo mouse tractography graphs and Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas tracer graphs to random geometric surrogate graphs that preserve each modality’s low-order distance effects.
ocar.resolution: Geometry plays a substantially larger role in tractography topology than in tracer graphs. Tractography underestimates long-distance weights and places hubs near the geometric center of the brain, as do tractography-derived surrogates, whereas tracer graphs place hubs further into peripheral cortex. Differences between two streamline node-assignment strategies were small relative to tractography-versus-tracer differences.
ocar.future_work: They urge geometric benchmarking in future tractography validation and caution for network measures that depend on long-range connections. A comparison passage argues the qualitative conclusion would persist if denser whole-brain empirical tracer measurements were available.

summaries.beginner: MRI can estimate brain wiring in living humans, but long fibers are easy to lose or mis-trace. By comparing mouse MRI maps with gold-standard tracer maps, this study shows that MRI networks look more like ‘nearby regions stick together’ geometry than the tracer networks do.
summaries.intermediate: Trinkle et al. (NeuroImage, 2021) use geometric surrogate graphs to isolate spatial embedding in mouse tractography versus Allen tracer networks. Tractography underestimates long-range weights, biasing hubs toward the geometric center and shaping modules and efficiency more like distance-preserving random graphs. Tracer graphs are less geometry-dominated. Two tractography assignment strategies differed little compared with the modality gap.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript. ‘Substantially larger role’ is qualitative in the extract; no single percentage of variance is given as a headline number. Ex vivo mouse tractography is not a human protocol. Gămănuţ et al. data are discussed as a limited extra tracer comparison.

plain_language_summary: MRI can estimate brain wiring in living humans, but long fibers are easy to lose or mis-trace. By comparing mouse MRI maps with gold-standard tracer maps, this study shows that MRI networks look more like ‘nearby regions stick together’ geometry than the tracer networks do.

ocar.opportunity: Activity is known to sculpt mammalian circuits; if the same is true in Drosophila, the fly toolkit could dissect how experience and spikes help assemble a stereotyped connectome.
ocar.challenge: Fly wiring was long treated as sufficiently explained by genetically hardwired cell-recognition molecules, leaving little room for developmental activity.
ocar.action: Akin and Zipursky, in Current Opinion in Genetics and Development (2020), as described in the catalog abstract, review recent evidence that activity during development contributes to circuit assembly in the fly.
ocar.resolution: The abstract concludes that activity is a fundamental aspect of brain development in general and that Drosophila offers opportunities to study the phenomenon through tools for circuit development, structure, and function.
ocar.future_work: How broadly activity acts across fly circuits, and how it interacts with recognition molecules, is the review’s implied agenda rather than a new experiment.

summaries.beginner: People used to think fruit-fly brains are wired by genes alone, like a fixed blueprint. This review says electrical activity during development also helps build fly circuits, so flies can be used to study that process.
summaries.intermediate: Akin and Zipursky (Current Opinion in Genetics and Development, 2020) review evidence that developmental activity contributes to Drosophila circuit assembly, contrary to a purely hardwired view based on cell-recognition molecules. They frame activity as a general feature of brain development and highlight the fly toolkit. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Voufo, Chen, Smith, Yan, Feller, and Tiriac, eLife (2023), on circuit mechanisms of embryonic (stage 1) mouse retinal waves, not Akin and Zipursky on fly developmental activity. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Current Opinion paper is required.

plain_language_summary: People used to think fruit-fly brains are wired by genes alone, like a fixed blueprint. This review says electrical activity during development also helps build fly circuits, so flies can be used to study that process.

ocar.opportunity: Most EM synapse maps of thalamus-to-cortex wires come from first-order sensory pathways; higher-order thalamic input to higher-order cortex may follow different ultrastructural rules.
ocar.challenge: Higher-order thalamocortical projections are harder to label without retrograde contamination, so their synapses are poorly described.
ocar.action: Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri, in European Journal of Neuroscience (2020), as described in the catalog abstract, combine intersectional viral labeling (cre plus cre-dependent ascorbate peroxidase) with large-volume serial EM of the mouse posterior medial nucleus projection to secondary somatosensory cortex.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports labeled thalamocortical synapses as 14% of all synapses in the volume, free of retrograde labeling in all cortical layers. Labeled terminals were larger, more often contained a mitochondrion, preferred spiny over aspiny dendrites, and often innervated larger spines with spine apparatuses. Labeled terminals were more prevalent in layers 2/3, and labeled-versus-unlabeled differences were greatest there, contrasting with first-order pathways where layer 4 terminals can be larger.
ocar.future_work: The abstract calls for more analyses, arguing such connectivity likely represents a majority of thalamocortical circuitry.

summaries.beginner: We know a lot about how first-order sensory thalamus talks to primary cortex, and much less about ‘higher-order’ thalamic messages. This study uses genetic labels plus electron microscopy in mouse to look at those higher-order synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Sampathkumar et al. (European Journal of Neuroscience, 2020), according to the catalog abstract, map posterior medial nucleus axons in secondary somatosensory cortex with intersectional APEX labeling and serial EM. Labeled synapses are reported as 14% of synapses in the volume; terminals are larger, mitochondrion-rich, spine-preferring, and especially different from unlabeled terminals in layers 2/3. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Iseri et al., a bioRxiv preprint (DOI 10.1101/2024.02.14.580149; stamp May 2026) on Aii amacrine rewiring in a pathoconnectome-based model of early retinal degeneration, not the Sampathkumar thalamocortical EM study. The 14% figure and ultrastructural contrasts above are from the catalog abstract only. Independent reading of the EJN paper is required.

plain_language_summary: We know a lot about how first-order sensory thalamus talks to primary cortex, and much less about ‘higher-order’ thalamic messages. This study uses genetic labels plus electron microscopy in mouse to look at those higher-order synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Nanometer-scale 3D maps of entire cells could quantify how dozens of organelle classes are arranged and interact, not only how neurons wire.
ocar.challenge: FIB-SEM whole-cell volumes are huge, and tens of organelle classes cannot be reconstructed by hand.
ocar.action: Heinrich, Bennett, Ackerman, and the COSEM Project Team, in a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, combine near-isotropic FIB-SEM (4 or 8 nm voxels) with deep learning trained on diverse samples to reconstruct 35 organelle classes.
ocar.resolution: Automatic reconstructions are used to quantify previously inaccessible metrics, including spatial interactions, and to register light and electron microscopy for correlative studies. They release OpenOrganelle (openorganelle.janelia.org) with raw data, training data, reconstructions, code, and models. A high-pressure-frozen HeLa cell at 4 nm isotropic voxels is shown as a complete whole-cell example, with manual blocks annotating up to 35 classes as ground truth.
ocar.future_work: They invite the community to query and further reconstruct the datasets. Detailed remaining-error analysis is referred to a Discussion section not fully present in the selected extract.

summaries.beginner: Cells are packed with many kinds of organelles that are hard to count in 3D. This Janelia preprint uses fine-scale electron microscopy and machine learning to draw 35 kinds of structures inside whole cells and shares the data as OpenOrganelle.
summaries.intermediate: Heinrich et al. / COSEM (bioRxiv, 2020) segment 35 organelle and macromolecular classes from whole-cell FIB-SEM at 4 or 8 nm voxels using deep networks trained across cell types. They emphasize spatial interaction metrics and automated LM–EM registration, and they open-source data and models via OpenOrganelle. The HeLa 4 nm volume is a flagship example. This is cell biology volume EM, not a neuronal wiring diagram.
summaries.advanced: Preprint (CC-BY). ‘35 classes’ and voxel sizes are stated in abstract and body. No single accuracy number for all classes is given as a headline in the selected text. Related-work citations are deferred to supplement. Later journal version is not this file.

plain_language_summary: Cells are packed with many kinds of organelles that are hard to count in 3D. This Janelia preprint uses fine-scale electron microscopy and machine learning to draw 35 kinds of structures inside whole cells and shares the data as OpenOrganelle.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM segmentation would move faster if networks could be pretrained on relevant unlabeled images, as in other vision fields.
ocar.challenge: Supervised ROI-trained models fail to generalize; existing EM pretraining sets are large, homogeneous, expensive, and weak for unseen biology.
ocar.action: Conrad and Narayan, in eLife (2021), release CEM500K, a 25 GB set of 0.5×10^6 unique 2D cellular EM images curated from nearly 600 3D and 10,000 2D images from more than 100 unrelated projects.
ocar.resolution: Models pretrained on CEM500K are reported to learn biologically relevant features that are resilient to meaningful augmentations. Transfer learning is reported as state-of-the-art on six public plus one new segmentation benchmarks. Data and code are at EMPIAR-10592 and a linked git repository. They argue 2D pretrained weights are broadly useful, including for labs with limited HPC.
ocar.future_work: 3D instance segmentation, common in connectomics, may need 3D pretraining; a 3D analogue of CEM500K is called out. The current set is still skewed toward mice and brain; more uncommon organisms, tissues, protocols, and acquisition parameters are requested.

summaries.beginner: Computer programs that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures usually fail on a new lab’s images. This paper releases a large mixed set of unlabeled EM snapshots so programs can practice first, then fine-tune on a specific job.
summaries.intermediate: Conrad and Narayan (eLife, 2021; catalog listed as bioRxiv) present CEM500K: about half a million unique 2D cellular EM images in 25 GB, drawn from >100 projects. They show pretrained features transfer to seven segmentation benchmarks at what they call state-of-the-art. Release is via EMPIAR and code. Catalog journal does not match the published eLife PDF.
summaries.advanced: ‘State-of-the-art on each’ is the authors’ evaluation claim; per-task scores live in tables not fully in the selected extract. 2D pretraining is explicitly weaker for 3D instance segmentation. Heterogeneity is still limited (mice, brain). MoCoV2 is mentioned as a 3D-capable algorithm not fully exploited here.

plain_language_summary: Computer programs that outline cells in electron-microscope pictures usually fail on a new lab’s images. This paper releases a large mixed set of unlabeled EM snapshots so programs can practice first, then fine-tune on a specific job.

ocar.opportunity: Digital dendrites that match real morpho-electric properties and connectivity would let modelers fill regions from few reconstructions and probe disease-related shape change.
ocar.challenge: Biological reconstructions are too few for many cortical types; prior synthesis often failed to reproduce diversity, electrophysiology, and network structure together.
ocar.action: Kanari, Dictus, Chalimourda, Van Geit, Coste, Shillcock, Hess, and Markram, in a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, apply a topological morphology descriptor (TMD) to synthesize cortical dendrites (TNS algorithm) and build a synthesized cortical column.
ocar.resolution: Synthesized dendrites are described as statistically indistinguishable from reconstructions in morpho-electrical properties and connectivity, and the synthesized column’s connectome as almost indistinguishable from a reconstructed column. They report that 15 to 20 reconstructed neurons of a type suffice to reproduce population diversity with TNS, versus thousands of morphologies expressed per type in a region. Transforming TMDs lets them simulate stress-related dendritic degeneration and resulting microcircuit defects.
ocar.future_work: Next steps named are whole regions (neocortex, thalamus, hippocampus), combinations of deformations, use of transcriptomic–electric–morphology datasets, and axonal-tree synthesis.

summaries.beginner: There are not enough manually traced neurons to fill a realistic digital cortex. This Blue Brain preprint grows artificial dendrites that statistically match real ones and then asks how diseased-looking branches would change the wiring of a column.
summaries.intermediate: Kanari et al. (bioRxiv, 2020) use topological barcodes of reconstructed cortical dendrites to synthesize statistically similar trees and a layered cortical column whose connectome they compare to a reconstructed column. A minimum of 15–20 reconstructions per type is stated for TNS diversity. TMD transformations model stress-related degeneration and its network-level effects. Axons are explicitly not solved.
summaries.advanced: Preprint; reuse restricted (‘no reuse without permission’) on the extract. ‘Statistically indistinguishable’ / ‘almost indistinguishable’ are authors’ summaries, not a single p-value in the selected text. Disease simulations are morphological transformations, not patient tissue. Blue Brain / EPFL affiliation.

plain_language_summary: There are not enough manually traced neurons to fill a realistic digital cortex. This Blue Brain preprint grows artificial dendrites that statistically match real ones and then asks how diseased-looking branches would change the wiring of a column.

ocar.opportunity: The rod bipolar pathway is a textbook night-vision circuit, but which interneurons supply most inhibition onto its central AII amacrine cell was unresolved.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic partners of AII cells that mediate long-range inhibition during scotopic vision needed combined anatomy and physiology, not connectivity lists alone.
ocar.action: Park, Lieberman, Ke, and colleagues, in a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, combine mouse retina connectomic and physiological analyses and confirm cell identity with nNOS-CreER.
ocar.resolution: Most synaptic inhibition onto AII amacrine cells is attributed to a single type: a multistratified, axon-bearing GABAergic amacrine cell with dendrites in ON and OFF layers but a pure ON light response, identified as the wide-field NOS-1 cell. Optogenetic stimulation of NOS-1 evoked AII IPSCs (normalized peak 39 ± 6 pA in a 60–70 ms window, n = 9) blocked by the GABA-A antagonist SR95531; NOS-1 cells also made synapses onto rod bipolars. Dopaminergic (TH+) amacrine cells did not overlap Cre-expressing NOS+ cells in the images shown.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame NOS-1 as a major rod-bipolar-pathway element for long-range inhibition in night vision; further roles beyond AII/RB inhibition are not a completed census in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Night vision in mammals funnels through a well-known chain of retinal cells, but it was unclear who applies most of the brakes on a key cell in that chain. This study finds one wide-field inhibitory cell type does most of that job.
summaries.intermediate: Park et al. (bioRxiv, 2020) report that NOS-1 amacrine cells provide the majority of synaptic inhibition to mouse AII cells, despite mixed ON/OFF dendrites and a pure ON light response. Identity is confirmed in nNOS-CreER tissue; optogenetics evoke GABAergic IPSCs in AIIs and inhibition in rod bipolars. They present this as connectomic discovery of a major night-vision interneuron.
summaries.advanced: Preprint. ‘Majority of synaptic inhibition’ is the authors’ anatomical/physiological conclusion; a full fraction is not restated as a single percentage in the selected extract beyond that qualitative claim. IPSC amplitude 39 ± 6 pA is for the optogenetic assay (n = 9). SBEM skeletonization assistance is acknowledged; this is not a whole-retina connectome paper.

plain_language_summary: Night vision in mammals funnels through a well-known chain of retinal cells, but it was unclear who applies most of the brakes on a key cell in that chain. This study finds one wide-field inhibitory cell type does most of that job.

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila connectomes propose monosynaptic premotor partners of the aCC motoneuron that still need functional tests with synaptic-timescale resolution.
ocar.challenge: Electrophysiology is rare in this CNS; behavior and GCaMP cannot prove monosynapticity. Driver lines may not label the intended neuron.
ocar.action: Giachello, Zarin, Kohsaka, Fan, Nose, Landgraf, and Baines, in a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, use electrophysiology, including TTX, to test GAL4 lines reported to label proposed aCC partners.
ocar.resolution: In the presence of TTX, A27h, A18a, A23a, and A31k are monosynaptically connected to aCC. Table 1 associates R36G02 (A27h-GAL4) with A27h and R15B07 (CLI2-GAL4) with A18a, among others. The authors stress that TTX-surviving responses are strong evidence for monosynapticity, while absence of TTX evidence is not definitive. Ectopic NaChBac in all cholinergic or GABAergic neurons was lethal; the method is limited to spiking neurons with ionotropic postsynaptic effects.
ocar.future_work: They highlight the need to validate driver lines before use. Metabotropic and graded synapses would be missed. This is not a full premotor census.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram can say two fly-larva neurons touch, but that is not the same as proving a working synapse. This paper uses electrical recordings, including a drug that blocks most network spikes, to confirm four premotor cells really talk directly to a named motor neuron.
summaries.intermediate: Giachello et al. (bioRxiv, 2020) electrophysiologically validate connectome-proposed premotor interneurons onto Drosophila larval aCC. Four types (A27h, A18a, A23a, A31k) remain coupled in TTX. Driver-line identity is treated as something that must be checked, not assumed. NaChBac pan-cholinergic or pan-GABAergic expression was lethal, limiting that alternative stimulation strategy.
summaries.advanced: Preprint. Monosynapticity is operationalized as TTX-resistant coupling, which the authors themselves note is asymmetric evidence. Table 1 in the extract is truncated after A18a lines. No new EM reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram can say two fly-larva neurons touch, but that is not the same as proving a working synapse. This paper uses electrical recordings, including a drug that blocks most network spikes, to confirm four premotor cells really talk directly to a named motor neuron.

ocar.opportunity: Nematode function is usually read from synaptic connectomes, but extrasynaptic volume transmission could explain signaling between cells that do not synapse.
ocar.challenge: No experiment had identified pseudocoelomic fluid as a vehicle for nematode neuropeptides. In Ascaris suum, FLP-18 peptides stimulate female reproductive organs yet are expressed far away without known synapses to that tissue.
ocar.action: Atkinson, Liu, McKay, and colleagues, in a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, analyze the A. suum PCF peptidome and its bioactivity on muscle, C. elegans receptors, and behavior.
ocar.resolution: As-PCF contains FMRFamide-like peptides and neuropeptide-like proteins, dominated by As-FLP-18A. It modulates nematode reproductive muscle ex vivo like synthetic FLP-18, activates C. elegans FLP-18 receptors NPR-4 and NPR-5, and alters C. elegans behavior. FLP-18 and receptors show pan-phylum distribution in nematodes.
ocar.future_work: They present this as the first direct evidence for an extrasynaptic volume route in nematodes and as relevant to receptor deorphanization and anthelmintic discovery. The extract’s later pages include broad species presence/absence tables rather than a mechanistic circuit model.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring diagrams show synapses, but peptides might also travel in the body fluid and act at a distance. This preprint finds such peptides in the body cavity of a parasitic nematode and shows they can drive muscle and worm behavior without needing a direct synapse.
summaries.intermediate: Atkinson et al. (bioRxiv, 2020) report extrasynaptic volume transmission via Ascaris suum pseudocoelomic fluid. The peptidome is dominated by As-FLP-18A; PCF mimics synthetic FLP-18 on reproductive muscle, activates NPR-4/5, and changes C. elegans behavior. Conservation across nematode species is used to argue pharmacological relevance. This expands the functional connectome beyond synapses.
summaries.advanced: Preprint. ‘First direct experimental evidence’ is the authors’ claim. Dominance of As-FLP-18A is qualitative in the abstract (‘dominates’). Species tables in the extract should not be read as quantitative expression levels. C. elegans connectome is background, not re-mapped.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring diagrams show synapses, but peptides might also travel in the body fluid and act at a distance. This preprint finds such peptides in the body cavity of a parasitic nematode and shows they can drive muscle and worm behavior without needing a direct synapse.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain C. elegans imaging is only comparable across animals if cells can be named, which would let functional data be pooled.
ocar.challenge: Unbiased identity assignment in dense stacks is expert-heavy; registration struggles when neurons are missing or postures vary.
ocar.action: Chaudhary, Lee, Li, Patel, and Lu, in eLife (2021 version of a 2020 DOI), introduce CRF_ID, a conditional-random-field framework that maximizes intrinsic shape similarity.
ocar.resolution: CRF_ID is reported to outperform existing methods on simulated and ground-truth experimental data and to be more robust to experimental noise. Atlases can be built from annotated data with cheap operations, and new features (for example from new strains) can be added. Demonstrations span strains, orientations, gene-expression localization, and multi-cell and whole-brain functional imaging. Missing neurons are said not to upset pairwise relationships among detected cells the way they hurt registration.
ocar.future_work: More animals, orientations, ages, and imaging techniques should improve generalizability. They suggest the approach may transfer to other systems whose tissues preserve relational geometry.

summaries.beginner: In worm whole-brain recordings, each glowing cell needs a name before experiments can be compared. This paper offers an automated naming method that looks at shapes and neighbor relationships instead of forcing every brain onto one template.
summaries.intermediate: Chaudhary et al. (eLife, 2021) present CRF_ID for automated annotation of C. elegans cell identities in dense images. The method uses conditional random fields on intrinsic similarity, optional data-driven atlases, and extra features from new strains. They report higher accuracy and noise robustness than registration-style baselines, including when neurons are missing and across postural orientations in microfluidic experiments.
summaries.advanced: Accuracy improvements are described qualitatively in the selected extract (figures cited, not a single headline percent). Catalog listed the work as bioRxiv; the PDF is eLife. This is identity assignment on light-microscopy volumes, not synapse reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: In worm whole-brain recordings, each glowing cell needs a name before experiments can be compared. This paper offers an automated naming method that looks at shapes and neighbor relationships instead of forcing every brain onto one template.

ocar.opportunity: Gap junctions in the Aii–ON cone bipolar cell network are essential for night vision, modulate day vision, and are implicated in oscillatory activity in retinal degenerations.
ocar.challenge: Extended coupling topology among ON bipolar classes, and whether it is conserved, was not well established; electrical synapses are easy to miss in connectomes.
ocar.action: Sigulinsky, Anderson, Kerzner, and colleagues, in Journal of Neuroscience (2020), map gap junctions in a high-resolution connectomics dataset of an adult female rabbit retina.
ocar.resolution: Gap junctions are 5%–25% of ON CBC axonal synaptic contacts. Uneven Aii-to-ON CBC coupling is conserved, including one class lacking direct Aii coupling. Unexpectedly, most ON CBC gap junctions are with other ON CBCs rather than with Aii cells, creating many within- and across-class lateral paths. Partnerships follow precise combination, size, and spatial rulesets that the authors compare to chemical-synapse specificity.
ocar.future_work: Whether disease oscillations use these normative motifs or novel ones is unknown. They provide partnership frequencies, sizing, and topology for future physiology and modeling, and argue that detecting coupling is necessary in connectomics studies.

summaries.beginner: Retinal cells share not only chemical synapses but also electrical pores. Mapping those pores in a rabbit retina, this study finds that ON bipolar cells are far more electrically networked with each other than the textbook Aii pathway alone would suggest.
summaries.intermediate: Sigulinsky et al. (Journal of Neuroscience, 2020) reconstruct gap junctions among ON cone bipolar cells in an adult female rabbit connectome. Junctions are 5–25% of ON CBC axonal contacts; Aii coupling is uneven and conserved, but most ON CBC gap junctions are CBC–CBC, with highly specific motifs within and across parallel channels. They argue this expands the Aii–ON CBC network for scotopic and photopic processing and for disease.
summaries.advanced: Single-animal, female rabbit volume; conservation claims compare to prior species literature. ‘Majority’ of ON CBC gap junctions being CBC–CBC is the authors’ count from this dataset. 5%–25% is a class range, not one number for all types. Disease-targeting implications are prospective.

plain_language_summary: Retinal cells share not only chemical synapses but also electrical pores. Mapping those pores in a rabbit retina, this study finds that ON bipolar cells are far more electrically networked with each other than the textbook Aii pathway alone would suggest.

ocar.opportunity: Each whisker maps to a cortical barrel, so cell-type-specific circuits in barrel cortex can be linked to tactile detection, texture, object location, and navigation.
ocar.challenge: How excitatory and inhibitory cell classes, local microcircuits, long-range connections, and neuromodulators implement whisker-guided behavior is still being assembled from many methods.
ocar.action: Staiger and Petersen, in Physiological Reviews (2020), as described in the catalog abstract, review pathways from whiskers to barrel cortex (wS1) and current knowledge of excitatory and inhibitory neuron types, synaptic connectivity, and cell-type-specific activity during behavior.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents wS1 as a well-defined map in which anatomical, electrophysiological, and molecular cell classes can be related to local and long-range connectivity and to behavior. An explicit goal is causal, mechanistic understanding of how selected tactile features are processed by specific neuron types and signaled downstream for sensory-guided decisions.
ocar.future_work: That causal, cell-type-specific account is named as a goal for future research rather than a completed result.

summaries.beginner: Mice and rats feel the world with whiskers, and each whisker has its own patch of cortex. This review gathers how those patches are built from different excitatory and inhibitory cells and how that may support touch-guided choices.
summaries.intermediate: Staiger and Petersen (Physiological Reviews, 2020), according to the catalog abstract, review neuronal circuits in rodent barrel cortex for whisker sensation. They cover ascending pathways, excitatory and inhibitory classes defined by anatomy, physiology, and molecules, local and long-range connectivity, neuromodulators, and links from cell-type activity to whisker behaviors. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Li, Chen, Geng, Zheng, Xie, Zhang, Cao, and Zhang, Research (2026), ‘A Corticotectal Pathway Regulates Vibrissal Somatosensory-Mediated Predatory Hunting Learning,’ not the Staiger and Petersen Physiological Reviews article. Claims above are from the catalog abstract only. Independent reading of the review is required.

plain_language_summary: Mice and rats feel the world with whiskers, and each whisker has its own patch of cortex. This review gathers how those patches are built from different excitatory and inhibitory cells and how that may support touch-guided choices.

ocar.opportunity: Computational models of cognition need a mesoconnectome with laminar and cell-class specificity, which is extremely hard to measure directly everywhere.
ocar.challenge: Whether spatial gene expression can predict cell-class- and layer-specific axonal projections, and which genes carry that signal, was untested at this scale.
ocar.action: Timonidis, Bakker, and Tiesinga, in Neuroinformatics (2020), train models on public volumetric gene expression and connectivity to predict mouse cell-class and layer-specific projections, using both individual genes and spatial co-expression modules.
ocar.resolution: Ridge (L2-regularized) regression had the highest cross-validated accuracy, with a median r² of 0.54, corresponding to a median ROC AUC of 0.89 for binarized projections. Two hundred spatial gene modules from dictionary learning and sparse coding yielded a median r² of 0.51. Gene-ontology enrichment of the most predictive genes implicated postsynaptic function.
ocar.future_work: They present the workflow for multimodal integration to improve predicted mesoconnectomes. It remains a prediction, not a fully measured cell-class connectome.

summaries.beginner: If you know which genes are on in each mouse brain region, how well can you guess the long-range wiring? This study trains models on public maps and finds gene patterns, especially ones tied to synapses, predict quite a lot of the projection pattern.
summaries.intermediate: Timonidis, Bakker, and Tiesinga (Neuroinformatics, 2020) predict cell-class- and layer-specific mouse axonal projections from volumetric gene expression. Ridge regression reaches median r² 0.54 (median AUC 0.89 when binarized); 200 spatial modules reach median r² 0.51. Top genes enrich for postsynaptic annotations. Public connectivity and expression volumes are the inputs.
summaries.advanced: Median r²/AUC are cross-validated summaries stated in the abstract; they are not voxel-wise guarantees. This does not replace tracer or EM measurement. Open-access Springer article; extract’s tail is the reference list.

plain_language_summary: If you know which genes are on in each mouse brain region, how well can you guess the long-range wiring? This study trains models on public maps and finds gene patterns, especially ones tied to synapses, predict quite a lot of the projection pattern.

ocar.opportunity: Three-dimensional and very large field-of-view EM is limited by acquisition time, and biological tissue is dose-sensitive, so fewer electrons per average pixel would help.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether random sparse scanning plus reconstruction would still support a key connectomics task: automated neuron segmentation.
ocar.action: Potocek, Trampert, Peemen, Schoenmakers, and Dahmen, in Microscopy and Microanalysis (2020), as described in the catalog abstract, demonstrate a workflow of sparse SEM acquisition, reconstruction by compressive sensing or neural networks, and deep-learning neuron segmentation.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that average dwell time per pixel can be reduced by a factor of 2–3, described as real-life confirmation of prior simulated-data results for a core connectomics segmentation application.
ocar.future_work: How far sparse sampling can be pushed for other tissues and for instance segmentation at scale is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can waste time parking the beam on every pixel. This methods paper tests skipping many pixels, filling the picture back in with algorithms, and still automatically tracing neurons—claiming a two- to three-fold time or dose saving.
summaries.intermediate: Potocek et al. (Microscopy and Microanalysis, 2020), according to the catalog abstract, combine random sparse SEM scanning with compressive-sensing or neural-network reconstruction and then deep-network segmentation of neuron structures. They report a 2–3× reduction in average dwell time per pixel on real data. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Athey, Sawmya, Meirovitch, Schalek, Potocek, Chandok, Peemen, Lichtman, Samuel, and Shavit, Applied Microscopy (2025), ‘Analysis of smart imaging runtime,’ a SmartEM end-to-end timing study, not the 2020 sparse-scan segmentation paper. The 2–3× dwell-time factor above is from the catalog abstract only. Independent reading of the Microscopy and Microanalysis article is required.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can waste time parking the beam on every pixel. This methods paper tests skipping many pixels, filling the picture back in with algorithms, and still automatically tracing neurons—claiming a two- to three-fold time or dose saving.

ocar.opportunity: Unidirectional and reciprocal chemical synapses play different roles; recent male and hermaphrodite C. elegans maps allow those motifs to be counted with synaptic multiplicity.
ocar.challenge: How reciprocal connections relate to communication, synapse number, in-degree, and sex differences needed a statistical treatment on updated connectomes.
ocar.action: Wright and Goltsev, in European Journal of Neuroscience (2020), analyze unidirectional and reciprocal pairs in male and hermaphrodite chemical connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Reciprocal connections provide communication among most neurons that have chemical synapses and comprise on average more synapses than unidirectional connections and than the connectome as a whole. Afferent connections onto high in-degree neurons have above-average synaptic multiplicity, increasing with in-degree. Males form two times fewer reciprocal connections among sex-shared neurons than hermaphrodites, but many reciprocal connections involving male-specific neurons. The authors interpret this as evidence for Hebbian structural plasticity.
ocar.future_work: Functional tests of that plasticity interpretation are outside this statistical analysis.

summaries.beginner: In the worm, some cell pairs send chemical synapses both ways and some only one way. Counting those patterns in males and hermaphrodites, this paper finds two-way links are unusually synapse-rich and that males wire shared cells less reciprocally than hermaphrodites.
summaries.intermediate: Wright and Goltsev (European Journal of Neuroscience, 2020) quantify unidirectional versus reciprocal chemical connections in both C. elegans sexes. Reciprocal pairs dominate communication among chemically synapsing neurons and have higher mean synapse counts. Synaptic multiplicity on afferents rises with postsynaptic in-degree. Sex-shared reciprocal connections are twofold fewer in males, who instead form many reciprocal links with male-specific neurons. Hebbian structural plasticity is an interpretation.
summaries.advanced: ‘Most neurons’ and ‘two times fewer’ are the authors’ summary statistics as stated; exact pair counts are not in the selected extract (which ends in the reference list). Chemical connectomes only; gap junctions are not this analysis. Plasticity is inferred from structure, not from a longitudinal experiment.

plain_language_summary: In the worm, some cell pairs send chemical synapses both ways and some only one way. Counting those patterns in males and hermaphrodites, this paper finds two-way links are unusually synapse-rich and that males wire shared cells less reciprocally than hermaphrodites.

ocar.opportunity: Motif over-representation is widely used to infer biological function, so the significance test itself needs to be statistically defensible.
ocar.challenge: Standard randomization tests are disputed, and exponential random graph models (ERGMs) were historically hard to fit to large biological networks.
ocar.action: Stivala and Lomi, in Applied Network Science (2021; arXiv 2020), apply ERGMs to an undirected protein–protein interaction network and to directed gene-regulatory networks of E. coli and yeast.
ocar.resolution: ERGMs indicate over-representation of triangles in the PPI network and of transitive triangles (feed-forward loops) in E. coli and yeast regulatory networks, confirming prior work including Milo et al. (2002). Under-representation of cyclic triangles (feedback loops) is reproduced by models that omit a cyclic-triangle parameter, so they argue the lack of feedback loops is a consequence of degree distributions, two-paths, and transitive closure rather than an ‘anti-motif.’ They present what they describe as the first ERGMs of a yeast regulatory network kept directed.
ocar.future_work: Code, configs, and datasets are released. Despite this paper sitting in a connectomics catalog, the analyses are PPI and gene regulation, not a neuronal wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: Biologists often ask whether a small wiring pattern appears more often than chance, but the usual chance models can mislead. This paper uses a more careful statistical family and finds that feed-forward loops really are extra common in some gene networks, while missing feedback loops may just follow from other network features.
summaries.intermediate: Stivala and Lomi (Applied Network Science, 2021) fit ERGMs to a PPI network and directed regulatory networks. They confirm triangle and feed-forward-loop over-representation and argue cyclic-triangle scarcity is explained by other included structures. Advances in estimation are cited as why ERGMs are newly practical. This is a methods-and-reanalysis paper on molecular networks.
summaries.advanced: No neuronal connectome is modeled in the extract. ‘Confirm prior research’ means motif conclusions, not identical p-values. Catalog year is 2020; the PDF is an arXiv v5 dated 9 Nov 2021 corresponding to the 2021 journal article.

plain_language_summary: Biologists often ask whether a small wiring pattern appears more often than chance, but the usual chance models can mislead. This paper uses a more careful statistical family and finds that feed-forward loops really are extra common in some gene networks, while missing feedback loops may just follow from other network features.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans offers a connectome plus whole-brain calcium imaging, a setting to relate synapse-level structure to network dynamics without assuming purely linear controllability.
ocar.challenge: Prior controllability analyses used linear network dynamics, which the real circuit may violate, and did not extract the control signals the network might apply to itself.
ocar.action: Fieseler, Zimmer, and Kutz, in Journal of the Royal Society Interface (2020), fit a global low-dimensional linear dynamical system actuated by temporally sparse control signals on whole-brain recordings.
ocar.resolution: The inferred control signals associate with previously expert-annotated behavioral transitions and can be predicted from neurons already implicated in those transitions plus additional neurons not previously associated with them. Failure to identify control signals during the forward state, and lower reconstruction quality there, is discussed as possibly due to insufficient data.
ocar.future_work: Longer recordings and more neurons may reveal forward-state control signals. Locally linear switching models are mentioned as an alternative. Code is released on GitHub.

summaries.beginner: Worm whole-brain recordings look like a high-dimensional movie of cell activity. This paper finds a few brief ‘control’ events that help explain switches between behaviors, and it points to neurons that could generate those events.
summaries.intermediate: Fieseler, Zimmer, and Kutz (J. R. Soc. Interface, 2020) model C. elegans whole-brain calcium data as sparse-input linear dynamics. Control pulses line up with expert behavioral transitions and are predictable from known plus additional neurons. The method is unsupervised with respect to those labels at discovery time, then compared to them. Forward locomotion is the regime with weaker recovered controls.
summaries.advanced: This is a dynamical model of imaging, not a new connectome. Biological interpretation of ‘control neurons’ is correlative/predictive. Data from Zimmer lab whole-brain recordings (Kaplan, Schrödel, Nichols acknowledged). MATLAB package cited.

plain_language_summary: Worm whole-brain recordings look like a high-dimensional movie of cell activity. This paper finds a few brief ‘control’ events that help explain switches between behaviors, and it points to neurons that could generate those events.

ocar.opportunity: Macro/meso connectomics and micro connectomics have been separate; a statistical neuron-to-neuron map of whole mouse neocortex could serve as a null model and a simulation substrate.
ocar.challenge: Combining region-to-region strengths with individual whole-brain axon reconstructions into predicted single-neuron innervation is non-trivial and incomplete in the data (for example GABAergic projection neurons).
ocar.action: Reimann, Gevaert, Shi, Lu, Markram, and Muller, in Nature Communications (2019), build a first-draft statistical model of the mouse whole-neocortex micro-connectome from meso-scale connectivity and whole-brain axon reconstructions.
ocar.resolution: They report a targeting principle that predicts individual-axon innervation logic from meso-scale data. The resulting connectome recreates biological targeting trends at macro, meso, and micro scales and predicts that scale-invariant topological organization of connectivity extends to individual neurons.
ocar.future_work: Code is at BlueBrain/Long-range-micro-connectome; axons from MouseLight. The model is a statistical draft, not an EM reconstruction. Layer profiles follow Harris et al.; GABAergic long-range cells are noted as missing from a constraining dataset.

summaries.beginner: We have coarse maps of which mouse cortical areas talk to which, and a smaller set of individually traced axons. This paper combines those ingredients into a first statistical guess at every neuron-to-neuron long-range connection in neocortex, meant as a baseline for simulations.
summaries.intermediate: Reimann et al. (Nature Communications, 2019) merge region-level connectivity with reconstructed axons to draft a mouse whole-neocortex micro-connectome. A targeting rule is used to predict how single axons innervate from meso data. They claim biological targeting trends are reproduced across scales and that scale-free topological organization continues to single neurons. It is offered as a null model and simulation substrate.
summaries.advanced: Not volume EM. ‘First draft statistical model’ is the authors’ framing. Open-access Nature Communications PDF. Python 2.7 construction code is dated. Constraints include Harris et al. layer profiles and MouseLight axons; GABAergic projections are a known gap.

plain_language_summary: We have coarse maps of which mouse cortical areas talk to which, and a smaller set of individually traced axons. This paper combines those ingredients into a first statistical guess at every neuron-to-neuron long-range connection in neocortex, meant as a baseline for simulations.

ocar.opportunity: Binary cortical graphs omit highly variable projection strengths that may shape both topology and dynamics.
ocar.challenge: How strength is placed on the macaque cortico-cortical network relative to small-world, modular, and rich-club organization was unclear.
ocar.action: de Lange, Ardesch, and van den Heuvel, in Network Neuroscience (2019), compare weighted and binary analyses of the Markov et al. (2014) macaque tract-tracing connectome and simulate interactions with the Kuramoto model.
ocar.resolution: Both weighted and binary versions show small-world, modular, and rich-club organization. Strength placement is nonrandom: relative to shuffled weights it increases clustering and characteristic path length via stronger modular structure, and it enhances the rich club’s role in global integration. Kuramoto simulations indicate that strength enhances synchronization within modules and among rich-club hubs.
ocar.future_work: The study is macaque retrograde/anterograde tracing, not EM. Generalization to other weighting schemes or species is not tested here.

summaries.beginner: A map that only says whether two brain areas are connected ignores how strong those pathways are. In the macaque, this paper finds that the strong pathways are not randomly assigned: they boost local grouping and the tightly linked hub core, and they make simulated activity more synchronized in those groups.
summaries.intermediate: de Lange, Ardesch, and van den Heuvel (Network Neuroscience, 2019) analyze Markov et al. (2014) macaque cortico-cortical strengths. Weighted and binary graphs share small-world, modular, and rich-club structure, but empirical weights augment clustering and rich-club integration versus random weight placement. Kuramoto dynamics show enhanced within-module and among-hub synchronization. Hub definition uses in-degree.
summaries.advanced: Tract-tracing FLNe-style weights, not MRI or EM. Comparisons to randomized weight placement and to min/max attainable measures are described in the extract; exact coefficient values are in figures/tables not fully reproduced. MIT Press open-access PDF with download watermark.

plain_language_summary: A map that only says whether two brain areas are connected ignores how strong those pathways are. In the macaque, this paper finds that the strong pathways are not randomly assigned: they boost local grouping and the tightly linked hub core, and they make simulated activity more synchronized in those groups.
